title: Predators and Prey Change Each Other's Numbers

scenes.visual: Island outline in Lake Superior with blue moose dots and two red wolf dots; counts appear; question writes in
scenes.tts: Isle Royale is an island in Lake Superior. Wolves hunt moose there. In the winter of twenty sixteen, scientists counted only two wolves on the whole island. They estimated one thousand three hundred moose. So here is the question. If wolves eat moose, why don't the wolves eat every last moose?
scenes.caption: Isle Royale is an island in Lake Superior. Wolves hunt moose there. In the winter of 2016, scientists counted only 2 wolves on the whole island. They estimated 1,300 moose. So here is the question. If wolves eat moose, why don't the wolves eat every last moose?
scenes.narration: Isle Royale is an island in Lake Superior. Wolves hunt moose there. In the winter of 2016, scientists counted only 2 wolves on the whole island. They estimated 1,300 moose. So here is the question. If wolves eat moose, why don't the wolves eat every last moose?

scenes.visual: Moose dots circled as a population; wolf chip tagged predator, moose chip tagged prey
scenes.tts: A population is all the members of one species living in one place. All the moose on the island are one population. A predator is an animal that catches and eats other animals. The animal it eats is its prey. Moose are the main prey of the island's wolves.
scenes.narration: A population is all the members of one species living in one place. All the moose on the island are one population. A predator is an animal that catches and eats other animals. The animal it eats is its prey. Moose are the main prey of the island's wolves.

scenes.visual: Chain balsam fir to moose to wolf with arrows from food to eater; a pack of wolves
scenes.tts: A food web shows who eats whom. Each arrow points from the food to the eater. Moose eat fir trees. When a wolf eats a moose, some of the energy stored in the moose passes to the wolf. Wolves often hunt moose as a pack. A pack is a group of predators that live and hunt together.

scenes.visual: Loop of four chips; many moose, then wolf dots increase, then moose dots fall
scenes.tts: Here is a pattern scientists often see. When prey are plentiful, predators find food easily. More predators survive and raise young. So the predator population grows. Then more predators catch more prey, and the prey population falls.
scenes.narration: Here is a pattern scientists often see. When prey are plentiful, predators find food easily. More predators survive and raise young. So the predator population grows. Then more predators catch more prey, and the prey population falls.

scenes.visual: Loop continues: wolves fall, moose rise; then a sketch of two curves, wolves a little after moose
scenes.tts: With less prey to eat, predators run short of food. Fewer of them survive, so the predator population falls. With fewer predators hunting, more prey survive. The prey population grows again. So predator numbers often rise and fall a little after prey numbers.
scenes.narration: With less prey to eat, predators run short of food. Fewer of them survive, so the predator population falls. With fewer predators hunting, more prey survive. The prey population grows again. So predator numbers often rise and fall a little after prey numbers.

scenes.visual: Other causes point into the counts; then wolves short of food, fewer wolves, moose recover; answer line
scenes.tts: Real populations are messier. On Isle Royale, harsh winters, ticks, disease and the moose's plant food also change the counts. Predators are one cause of change, not the only one. Still, predators usually run short of food before the last prey animal is caught. Then fewer wolves survive, and the moose can recover. That is why wolves do not eat every last moose.
